Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Aegis Insurance Group Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star two. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Jenkins, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Aegis Insurance Group's Q2 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Rivera, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Underwriting Officer; and Robert Kline, Chief Investment Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we are making today may be considered forward-looking. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those projected. We encourage you to review our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties.

I will now turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on Aegis Insurance Group's performance for Q2 2024. We delivered strong results, driven by robust investment income yields, elevated policy retention rates across major product lines, favorable changes in actuarial assumptions, significant reinsurance recoveries both received and expected, and a sharp improvement in our combined ratio overall and by segment. Our focus on disciplined portfolio management, data-driven underwriting, and strategic reinsurance placements continues to yield positive outcomes, positioning us well for sustained growth and shareholder value creation.

Michael, our CFO, will now provide a more detailed review of our financial performance.

Michael Rivera: Thank you, Johnathan. Good morning, everyone. As Johnathan mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Our net income was $350 million, or $1.85 per share. Key drivers of our financial performance included higher investment yields, strong retention adding to premium run-rates, assumption updates releasing reserves, reinsurance cash flows, and underwriting discipline reflected in our ratios. Our combined ratio was 94.6%, reflecting effective underwriting and claims management. Investment income for the quarter was $285 million. We continue to maintain a strong capital position, with an RBC ratio of 520%.

Let me dive deeper into these areas, starting with our investment income yield, a core driver of our earnings power and a testament to our disciplined portfolio management in a volatile fixed income environment. For those less familiar, investment income yield represents our net investment income—including interest, dividends, and realized gains net of impairments—divided by our average invested assets, expressed as a percentage. It's a key metric for insurers like us, as it directly impacts our spread business between earned premiums and claims, while supporting competitive pricing on products like fixed annuities and whole life policies.

In Q2 2024, our annualized investment income yield came in at 4.25%, up 45 basis points year-over-year from 3.80% in Q2 2023, and a sequential improvement of 12 basis points from Q1's 4.13%. On a trailing 12-month basis, we're now at 4.18%, marking our strongest full-year performance since the pre-pandemic era. This translated to that $285 million in net investment income for the quarter, a 14% increase year-over-year, on average invested assets of $28.7 billion—up modestly from $27.9 billion a year ago, reflecting steady cash flows from our P&C and life & annuity segments.

What's driving this outperformance? First and foremost, the higher-for-longer rate environment. The Fed's terminal rate around 5.25-5.50% has pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.35% as of quarter-end, up from 3.85% a year ago, allowing us to reinvest maturing securities at materially higher book yields. Our new money yield—the rate on fresh investments—averaged 5.12% in Q2, compared to 4.65% in the prior-year period. This is particularly accretive to our longer-duration life & annuity book, where liabilities have an average duration of 8.2 years, giving us a natural tailwind from the yield curve steepening.

Portfolio-wise, fixed maturities remain our bedrock at 78% of the portfolio, or $22.4 billion, yielding 4.45%—up from 3.92% year-over-year. We've maintained an investment-grade bias, with 92% rated BBB or higher per S&P, minimizing credit spread compression risks amid narrow corporate spreads at 105 basis points over Treasuries. Taxable municipals, at 12% of fixed income, delivered a tax-equivalent yield of 5.1%, benefiting from strong municipal demand and our active secondary market trading. Corporate bonds are skewed toward financials at 22% and utilities at 18%, sectors we've overweighted for their defensive yields and low default rates—historical probability of default at just 0.4% for our holdings.

Equities and alternatives round out the picture at 15% and 7%, respectively. Our equity sleeve, managed via index-linked strategies mirroring the S&P 500 and dividend aristocrats like those in the ProShares S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats ETF, yielded 3.2% including dividends, with minimal volatility thanks to our 1.2x beta cap. Alternatives—including core REITs like Prologis and infrastructure via Brookfield funds—contributed a robust 6.8% yield, hedging against inflation in our property casualty lines.

Regionally, our U.S. portfolio, which is 72% of assets under management, drove the yield lift to 4.38%, fueled by domestic rate hikes and our $1.2 billion deployment into agency MBS at spreads of 110 basis points over swaps. Europe, at 18% of assets, lagged slightly at 3.95% due to the ECB's more dovish stance—with German bunds at 2.45%—but our opportunistic shift into UK gilts yielding 4.1% and peripheral sovereigns has narrowed the gap. Asia-Pacific, 10% of the book, yielded 4.05%, supported by JGBs and AUD corporates amid RBA hawkishness, though we're monitoring China's property sector exposure closely, capped at under 2% with hedges via credit default swaps.

Strategically, we've leaned into several technical initiatives to sustain this momentum. One is active duration management: our portfolio duration is now 5.8 years, down from 6.4 years last year, via targeted sales of long-dated Treasuries and a $450 million ladder extension program locking in 4.75%+ rates out to 2030. We've also ramped ESG integration—28% of new fixed income allocations are SFDR Article 8 or 9 compliant—without sacrificing yield, targeting green bonds from issuers like Chubb's sustainability-linked notes. On the derivative front, we've deployed $800 million in interest rate swaps to extend effective duration synthetically, capturing forward curve value while matching asset-liability management mismatches in our variable annuity guarantees.

Derisking remains paramount: unrealized losses narrowed to $1.4 billion pre-tax from $2.1 billion year-over-year, with held-to-maturity securities at 35% of fixed income shielding other comprehensive income volatility. Compared to peers, our yield outperforms Allstate's 3.95% and Progressive's 4.05% trailing yields, though trails Berkshire's 4.6% due to their equity overweight—a trade-off we're comfortable with given our liability profile.

Looking forward, we expect Q3 yield to hold in the 4.3-4.4% range, assuming 10-year yields stabilize around 4.2%. Risks include Fed cuts—we've stress-tested for a 100 basis point drop, projecting a 25 basis point yield hit—and credit migration, but our 200 basis point investment spread over liabilities provides ample cushion. Our capital deployment plan includes $2-3 billion in new investments over the next year, prioritizing high-conviction sectors like securitized products and private credit via partnerships with Blackstone and Apollo.

In summary on this front, our investment income yield underscores Aegis's fortress balance sheet and ALM expertise, fueling ROE expansion to 13.2% this quarter.

Turning now to policy retention rates by major product line, another critical leading indicator of customer loyalty, lifetime value, and our ability to compound earned premiums without the drag of high acquisition costs. Retention is the lifeblood of our P&C and life franchises, directly impacting our combined ratio and return on equity. In Q2, we delivered an overall retention rate of 89.2%, up 140 basis points year-over-year and marking our 11th straight quarter of sequential improvement. This outperforms the industry average of 85-87% as reported by JD Power and AM Best benchmarks, reflecting the strength of our data-driven pricing, digital servicing, and proactive renewal strategies.

Breaking this down by our major product lines, with some color on trends, regional nuances, and the initiatives driving these results. In Personal Lines Auto Insurance, our retention came in at 87.5%, a robust 210 basis points improvement year-over-year from 85.4%. This is ahead of peers like Progressive and Geico, who have hovered around 84-86% amid softening commercial auto rates. The uptick is fueled by our Snapshot telematics program, now with 28% penetration in our book—up from 22% a year ago—which rewards safe driving with up to 30% discounts at renewal. We've seen a 15% reduction in attrited policies from high-risk drivers due to personalized feedback loops via our app. Inflationary pressures on repair costs have pushed loss ratios to 72%, but our usage-based insurance model has stabilized severity trends. Regionally, U.S. retention hit 88.2%, bolstered by bundling with home policies in multi-product households now 62% of our auto book. In Europe, it's 85.1%, pressured by regulatory rate caps in the UK post-FCA pricing reforms, but our AI-powered renewal optimizer is clawing back 200 basis points there.

Homeowners retention was exceptional at 92.3%, up 90 basis points year-over-year, significantly outpacing Allstate's reported 89% and driven by catastrophe resilience. Renters held steady at 88.7%. Key here is our Smart Home initiative, integrating IoT sensors for 12% of policyholders, which has cut claims frequency by 18% through predictive risk mitigation—think leak detection and wildfire alerts in California. Amid Reinsurance Association of America warnings on hardening cat reinsurance markets, we've maintained discipline with 5% rate adequacy increases, minimizing shock lapses. U.S. Southeast retention is 93.1%, benefiting from post-Hurricane Ian rebuild loyalty programs, while our emerging Asia book, like India via our HDFC Ergo JV, is at 82.4%, improving via localized micro-insurance bundles but challenged by monsoon seasonality.

In Commercial Lines Property & Casualty, retention improved to 84.6%, a 160 basis points year-over-year gain from 83.0%, aligning with Travelers' mid-80s but ahead of smaller regionals facing mid-70s churn. Middle-market retention, premiums $25K-$250K, led at 86.2%, thanks to our Industry-X platform, which uses machine learning for real-time exposure modeling—reducing non-renewals from basis risk mismatches by 22%. Workers' Comp specifically retained 85.1%, supported by our Return-to-Work partnerships with 4,500 employers, slashing indemnity costs. Challenges persist in excess & surplus lines at 79.8%, where capacity influx from Lloyd's and Bermuda reinsurers has commoditized pricing. Regionally, North America shines at 85.9% with strong small business loyalty post-COVID, Europe at 82.3% amid EU Solvency II capital strains, and LatAm at 78.5%, where we're investing in agent digitization to counter informal market competition.

Rounding out the portfolio, Life retention was 94.1%—our highest ever, up 70 basis points year-over-year—driven by persistency in term life at 95.2% and universal life at 93.4%. This beats Prudential's 92-93% peers, reflecting our no-lapse guarantee riders and embedded financial planning tools in the myAegis app, which boosted surrender rates down 8%. Annuities held at 96.7%, resilient despite fixed indexed product outflows amid rising rates. U.S. dominance at 94.8% contrasts with Asia's 91.2%, where regulatory shifts in China are testing group life books, but our bancassurance channels via partners like DBS Bank are stabilizing flows.

These retention gains have added about $450 million to our in-force premium run-rate year-to-date, directly supporting a 95.8% renewal pricing capture rate. Technically, our EagleEye AI suite—now covering 75% of renewals—dynamically adjusts for loss trends, telematics data, and macroeconomic signals like CPI inflation currently at +3.2%, preventing adverse selection. We've also rolled out "Retention 95"—a cross-sell engine targeting 10% uplift in multi-line penetration by 2025, inspired by digital playbooks but scaled for our $45 billion book. Regionally, mature markets like the U.S. and Canada blended at 90.1% benefit from high digital adoption—65% self-service renewals—while growth markets blended at 82.7% require hybrid agent-tech models. Looking forward, we guide to 89.5-90.5% full-year overall retention, assuming no major cat events, with upside from Q3 bundling campaigns. This positions us for mid-teens ROE expansion as acquisition costs remain about 25% of premiums.

Next, I'd like to address changes in actuarial assumptions and their impact on our financials. These underpin our liability valuations across our Life & Annuity, Group Health, and Property & Casualty segments. They're recalibrated quarterly based on emerging experience data, economic shifts, and regulatory feedback from bodies like the NAIC, EIOPA, and OSFI.

In Q2, we recorded a net favorable impact of $285 million pre-tax from assumption updates, contributing roughly 15 basis points to our core return on equity. This compares to a $112 million unfavorable hit in Q2 2023, when higher inflation and post-COVID morbidity trends pressured our books. Let's break this down by key categories.

Our biggest mover this quarter was the discount rate uplift, driven by the Fed's terminal rate settling around 4.25-4.50% amid cooling inflation data. For our $450 billion Life & Annuity block—dominated by fixed indexed annuities and universal life products—we increased our best-estimate discount rate by 25 basis points to 4.1% from 3.85%. This released $180 million in reserves, as higher rates reduce the present value of future liabilities. Regionally, this was amplified in the U.S., where 85% of our FIA sales flow through our Midwest and Southeast agencies. In contrast, our European operations under Solvency II saw a more modest 15 basis points bump to 3.2%, reflecting ECB rates hovering at 3.75%. Asia-Pacific, via our joint venture with Ping An Insurance, benefited less at $22 million favorable, as yields on JGBs and A-bonds remain suppressed. Strategically, we've layered in interest rate swaps hedging 70% of our FIA crediting strategies—locking in spreads above 120 basis points. Looking forward, if the yield curve steepens as projected by the CME FedWatch Tool, we expect another $200-250 million tailwind in Q3.

Mortality experience continues to normalize post the 2020-2022 COVID spike. Our updated Society of Actuaries scale—blending Scale 2022 with our proprietary Aegis Mortality Model—showed actual-to-expected ratios improving to 92% from 98% last year across our term life and whole life portfolios. This drove a $65 million favorable release, primarily in Group Life at $42 million, where we've seen A/E drop to 89% in our employer-sponsored plans. For longevity in our pension risk transfer business—$120 billion in force—we extended ultimate mortality improvements by 0.5% annually, reflecting Blue Zone studies and GLP-1 drug impacts on obesity-related claims. This added a $15 million reserve strengthen, prudently offsetting tail risks. Regionally, U.S. Southeast states like Florida and Texas saw elevated A/E at 95% due to hurricane-linked comorbidities, while our UK block under PRA scrutiny benefited from NHS data showing 2% faster longevity convergence. In Canada, OSFI-mandated dynamic lapsing models cushioned us by $8 million.

In Group Health and Disability—23% of reserves—we lowered morbidity assumptions by 3% based on claims data from our stop-loss and voluntary benefits products. Post-pandemic elective surgeries rebounded, but Ozempic-like therapies reduced diabetes claims by 12%, mirroring UnitedHealth's trends. This unlocked $48 million favorable. Lapse rates ticked up 1.5% to 8.2% in UL and variable annuities, driven by equity market gains—S&P 500 up 22% year-to-date—prompting policyholder surrenders. While this strengthened reserves by $22 million, we offset it with anti-lapse features in new FIAs, targeting 95% persistency. Expenses held steady, but we trued up inflation at 2.8% down from 4.2%, saving $10 million, aided by our GenAI-powered claims adjudication platform, which cut processing costs 18% year-over-year.

Shifting to Property & Casualty, where cat losses from events like Hurricanes Helene and Milton totaled $450 million gross, we updated severity assumptions upward 5% for coastal windstorm deductibles, per RMS v18 models. This reserved an additional $18 million unfavorable, concentrated in Florida 60% of exposure. However, favorable auto frequency trends—down 4% amid EV adoption—released $12 million net positive. Our reinsurance tower, placed with Swiss Re and Munich Re at a 28% cession rate, mitigated 75% of this volatility.

Under IFRS 17, these changes boosted our Contractual Service Margin by $210 million, with risk adjustment stable at 8% of best estimate liability. U.S. statutory reserves fell 1.2%, enhancing our RBC ratio to 520% from 485%, well above the 400% target. We've proactively filed our annual assumption study with the NAIC, incorporating climate risk overlays per SSAP 112. These updates reflect our "Experience + Forward-Looking" framework, leveraging 15 petabytes of telematics and wearable data via our Actuarial AI Hub—partnered with Palantir for predictive modeling. We're ahead of peers in embedding ESG factors, such as 10% higher loss trends for flood-prone assets. Forward, we guide to $900 million-$1.1 billion in net favorable assumption impacts for FY24, assuming no recession. Risks include persistent high rates eroding FIA sales or a morbidity reversal if flu seasons intensify. Mitigants: expanding PRT pipelines to $20 billion and piloting parametric reinsurance for Asia typhoons.

Now, on reinsurance recoveries received and expected, a critical component of our P&C underwriting results, particularly against elevated catastrophe activity. Reinsurance recoveries represent amounts we collect from our reinsurers under quota share, excess-of-loss, and catastrophe treaties for paid losses and loss adjustment expenses. These are netted against our gross incurred losses in the combined ratio calculation, directly impacting our loss ratio and overall expense discipline. In Q2, we continued to benefit from our diversified reinsurance program, renewed January 1st at favorable terms—averaging a 5.5% rate-on-line reduction from the prior year, thanks to our strong loss-free record on the 1/1/23 book and proactive cedent negotiations.

We received $478 million in cash recoveries during the quarter, a robust 28% increase from $373 million in Q2 2023. This was driven by settlements on prior-period catastrophe events, including Hurricane Ian residuals from 2022 and California wildfire claims from the 2023 season. Breaking it down by layer: Quota share treaties covering about 40% of our gross written premium contributed $192 million, or 40% of total receipts, primarily from our proportional programs on U.S. commercial auto and workers' comp lines, where recovery rates exceeded 95% of ceded paid losses. Excess-of-loss layers protecting tail risk above $100 million per event delivered $215 million, fueled by cat recoveries—$120 million alone from European storm claims under our XL program with Munich Re and Swiss Re. Industry loss warranty triggers added $71 million from binary triggers tied to industry losses exceeding $10 billion for North Atlantic named storms, which activated fully on Ian run-off.

This strong cash inflow reduced our net loss ratio by 420 basis points quarter-over-quarter, helping us achieve a Q2 accident-year combined ratio of 92.4%, ex-cats. Year-to-date, cumulative receipts stand at $892 million, pacing 15% ahead of our initial full-year guidance.

Looking forward, we expect to collect another $650-750 million in recoveries through December 31st, with $350 million probable within the second half and the balance contingent on case reserve developments. This pipeline is conservatively booked at a 92% ultimate recovery rate on ceded incurred losses, factoring in collateral adequacy and reinsurer credit quality—our program is 100% collateralized or rated A+ or better by AM Best. Key components: $280 million expected from favorable reserve releases on 2022-2023 attritional losses, bolstered by our actuarial teams' use of chain ladder and Bornhuetter-Ferguson methodologies, which have consistently outperformed peer benchmarks. Current-year cats: $220-320 million tied to Q2 events like Hurricane Beryl estimated industry loss $12-15 billion and European floods, under our peak peril covers up to $1.2 billion xs $150 million. IBNR tail: $150 million provisional for unpaid balances, with sensitivity to inflation in repair costs—we've stress-tested this at +10% severity, which only compresses our expected recovery rate to 88%.

Full-year total recoveries are now projected at $1.54-1.64 billion, up from our prior guidance of $1.4 billion, reflecting faster-than-expected settlements. Over the past 24 months, recoveries have trended upward at a 22% CAGR, outpacing gross loss growth due to our shift toward higher attachment points and multi-year deals. This quarter's performance aligns with industry patterns—per Swiss Re's sigma report, global reinsurance markets saw $110 billion in cat losses year-to-date, with cedants recovering about 75% on average. We're outperforming at 82% net recovery rate, thanks to our tech initiatives.

Regionally: U.S. 62% of recoveries with $295 million received year-to-date from Southeast wind and Western wildfire perils—Beryl alone positions us for $80-100 million, leveraging our facultative placements with Berkshire Hathaway. Europe 22% at $105 million from Storm Henk and flood events, under our pan-European excess program; strong recoveries here reflect tighter E.U. regulatory scrutiny under Solvency II, where we've optimized collateral via letters of credit. Asia-Pacific 10% at $48 million from Japan typhoons, with growth potential as we expand our A&H quota shares amid rising secondary perils. Rest of World 6% LatAm flood residuals, where we've initiated weather derivative overlays to hedge volatility.

We've invested heavily in our reinsurance management platform—integrating Guidewire's Reinsurance Management module with AI-driven predictive analytics from our proprietary 'ReCovAI' tool. This has slashed settlement cycles from 180 to 90 days, improving days payable outstanding by 15 points and freeing up $200 million in working capital year-to-date. On the strategic front, we're proactively diversifying away from Bermuda capacity now less than 15% of program toward U.S. and European reinsurers, mitigating collateral risks post-2023 Bermuda capital shocks. Looking ahead, these recoveries will support our 2025 renewal strategy: targeting flat-to-down rates on non-cat lines while maintaining robust cat protection at 50% quota share on peak zones. This positions us for a mid-90s combined ratio in a $150 billion industry market hardening on secondary perils.

Finally, let's cover our combined ratio analysis, both overall and by segment, which remains the cornerstone of our property and casualty underwriting discipline. The combined ratio is our gold standard profitability metric: it's the sum of our loss and loss adjustment expense ratio, or loss ratio, and our underwriting expense ratio. A combined ratio below 100% generates an underwriting profit; above it, a loss. We target a mid-90s accident year combined ratio over the cycle, excluding catastrophes, to deliver superior returns in this capital-intensive industry.

Our overall combined ratio for Q2 came in at 94.6%, a 210 basis point improvement from 96.7% in Q2 2023 and 50 basis points better than our Q1 2024 result of 95.1%. Year-to-date, we're at 94.8%, down 180 basis points year-over-year from 96.6%. This marks our best first-half performance since 2019, pre-COVID disruptions, and puts us on track for a full-year combined ratio of 95.5% to 96.5%, assuming normalized catastrophe activity.

Breaking it down, our Q2 loss ratio was 68.2%, down 150 basis points year-over-year, driven by earned premium growth outpacing paid losses, favorable prior-year development, and moderating severity trends. Our expense ratio held steady at 26.4%, reflecting disciplined cost management amid commission pressures from agency growth. Catastrophe losses totaled $285 million pre-tax, or 4.2 points on the ratio—in line with our 4-5 point quarterly guidance but elevated due to California wildfires and Midwest convective storms. Excluding cats, our underlying combined ratio was a pristine 90.4%, underscoring the strength of our core book.

Drilling into the segments: Personal Lines—52% of premiums, Q2 combined ratio 91.8% versus 94.2% year-over-year. Personal Lines delivered another standout quarter, with year-to-date at 92.1%, beating our 93% target. Auto was the star: 89.5% combined, fueled by telematics penetration now at 28% of policies—up from 22% a year ago—which has reduced loss frequency by 12% in our Snapshot program, with our proprietary AI-driven behavioral scoring. Homeowners came in at 95.2%, pressured by 7% repair cost inflation from labor shortages and materials, but offset by 9.5% average rate increases and stricter underwriting in high-hazard zones like Florida post-Hurricane Ian. Trend-wise, auto severity is stabilizing after peaking at +15% year-over-year in 2023 due to parts inflation and rental car exposure; we're now seeing +8% as supply chains normalize. Regionally, our Northeast book benefited from mild winter weather, while California wildcats added 2 points—we've responded with enhanced wildfire mitigation credits, partnering with Cal Fire for defensible space discounts, reducing exposure by 15% in at-risk tiers.

Commercial Lines—28% of premiums, Q2 combined ratio 98.2% versus 101.5% year-over-year. Commercial improved to year-to-date 97.9%, our best in three years, though still above our 96% goal due to large risk volatility. Middle-market P&C, our bread-and-butter, hit 96.8%, with workers' comp shining at 93.2% thanks to return-to-office trends curbing claims frequency. General liability, however, landed at 102.1%, hit by social inflation—jury awards up 18% per VerdictSearch data—and excess verdicts in trucking exposures. We've launched a technical overhaul here: Our "RiskOptix" platform, using machine learning for adverse selection detection, has cut attritional losses by 4 points since rollout. Compared to peers like Travelers, our commercial auto severity is +10% year-over-year but contained via earned loss ratio caps and telematics mandates for fleets over $5 million premium. Regionally, Europe—12% of this segment—saw a 95.4% ratio, boosted by 11% rate in the UK motor market amid Bodily Injury claim spikes, while Asia-Pacific at 99.8% faced Thailand floods, prompting reinsurance tower enhancements with partners like Swiss Re.

Specialty Lines—15% of premiums, Q2 combined ratio 96.5% versus 98.9% year-over-year. Specialty continues to anchor profitability at year-to-date 95.8%, with directors & officers at 94.2%—resilient despite Side A DIC demand post-FTX fallout—and cyber at 97.1%. Cyber's improvement stems from our "CyberGuard AI" initiative, which flags 25% more ransomware indicators at quote stage, reducing net losses by $45 million year-to-date. We've ceded 40% of cyber risk to our quota share with Munich Re, stabilizing volatility. Trends show cyber frequency up 22% per CyberCube analytics, but our attachment points and sub-limits have held severity flat. In marine cargo, Red Sea disruptions added 1.5 points regionally, but our hull portfolio in the Nordics remains sub-95% via predictive weather routing tech.

Reinsurance and Other—5% of premiums, Q2 combined ratio 105.3% versus 108.7% year-over-year. This tail segment, including assumed treaty business, improved to year-to-date 104.8% but reflects retrocession costs from US cat activity. We've optimized here by non-renewing 20% of underperforming retro layers, targeting sub-100% by year-end.

Across the board, earned rate is +9.2% year-over-year, outpacing $12.5 billion in premium growth 11% year-over-year. Loss trends are bending positively: Auto frequency -3%, severity +7%; property severity +5% ex-inflation. Inflation remains headwind—auto parts +9%, construction +6% per RSMeans data—but our vendor partnerships with O'Reilly Auto and Home Depot for direct repair networks cap it. Cat outlook: RMS v18 models project $120 billion industry US cat load for 2024; we've fortified with a 1:3:4 structure on our $2.5 billion tower, collateralized via Everest Re, shaving 50 basis points off ceded costs. Technically, our catastrophe response time is down 18% via drone claims tech, accelerating reserves. Strategically, we're doubling down on "Precision Underwriting 2.0": Integrating climate risk scores from Jupiter Intelligence into every quote, exiting 8% of coastal exposure profitably. Retention hit 87.2%, up 120 basis points, via loyalty pricing. Compared to Allstate's personal lines reset or The Hartford's commercial pivot, our multi-segment balance de-risks us—no single line >52% of book. ROE accretion from underwriting gains supports 12-14% targets, with excess capital for M&A like our bolt-on in Australian SMB P&C.

These elements collectively drove our strong quarter.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Michael. I'd like to provide an update on our underwriting performance. We've seen continued strong performance in our personal and commercial lines, with retention and combined ratio improvements as Michael detailed. We are actively managing our exposure to catastrophe risks and secondary perils like cyber and social inflation, and have implemented several initiatives like AI-driven risk selection, telematics expansion, and IoT integrations to improve our overall risk profile and support ongoing margin expansion.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from David Wong with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

David Wong: Good morning. Can you provide more color on the investment income yield outlook, especially with potential Fed cuts?

Robert Kline: Good morning, David. As Michael noted, we're guiding Q3 to 4.3-4.4%, with our stress tests showing resilience even in a 100 basis point drop scenario. Our new money yields at 5.12% and duration management give us a buffer, and we'll continue deploying into high-conviction areas like private credit.

Operator: Our next question comes from Emily Carter with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter: Good morning. Could you discuss the impact of higher rates on policy retention in life and annuities?

Michael Rivera: Good morning, Emily. Retention there held strong at 94.1% overall, with annuities at 96.7% despite some FIA outflows. Our no-lapse features and app-based planning tools have kept surrenders low, and we see bundling as a key upside.

Operator: Our next question comes from Raj Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Raj Patel: What is the expected impact of recent cat events on your combined ratio guidance and reinsurance recoveries?

Lisa Chen: Good morning, Raj. Cats added 4.2 points this quarter, but our ex-cat underlying is 90.4%, and recoveries of $478 million received helped. We expect $650-750 million more, supporting our full-year combined ratio guide of 95.5-96.5%. Our tower is robust for the remainder of the season.

Operator: Our next question comes from Sophia Lee with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Sophia Lee: Thanks. On actuarial assumptions, how sensitive are you to further mortality improvements or rate changes?

Michael Rivera: Hi Sophia. The $285 million favorable was broad-based, with discount rates the big driver. We've built in conservative longevity extensions, and our AI hub helps us stay ahead. FY24 guide is $900 million to $1.1 billion net favorable.

Operator: Seeing no further questions at this time, I'll turn it back to the company for closing remarks.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you for your questions and your interest in Aegis Insurance Group. In closing, we are confident in our ability to continue delivering strong results and creating value for our shareholders, backed by our investment performance, retention strength, assumption discipline, reinsurance support, and underwriting excellence. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
